summary: Round-6 review of a decomposition commit (no code). The four cuts named by the task are complete and I could find no surviving duplicate of any of them: no 'one GET' claim anywhere under ### M4.10*, no 'M4.10c is void' conditional attached to the SegmentKey observation, no instruction to run Invariants.checkChain, no golden-discrimination or anchor-both-directions paragraph. Most remaining facts check out against source, and I verified each one myself rather than accepting it: SegmentKey.render's field order and SegmentPublisher's 'unique WITHOUT coordination' comment (ingest/.../SegmentPublisher.java:130-137) with sequence an instance AtomicLong (:53); DefaultIngest.flushSeq an instance field (:63) incremented unconditionally at the sole production issuance site (:349); Checkpoint's own MAGIC/VERSION, no kind byte, decode comparing against one constant (format/.../Checkpoint.java:47-49,150-153) and CheckpointCursor.newest letting that IOException out (sequencer/.../CheckpointCursor.java:72-81) where BinStore:36 defines it as unreachable; the M3.0 quotation is faithful to backlog-done.md:93; ADR-0031 really is two live processes at the lease level; CheckpointWriter.pods is an uneviected HashMap folded with Math::max over a bare podId (:78,:130); ChainReplay:441 merges lastOffset+1 with Math::max; CommitLog PUTs and returns the same CommitDelta (:328-333); Invariants uses delta.runs() (:116,:253) and tracks only per-RunKey offsets, so both measured claims about it hold; CheckpointWriterContentTest really replays 9 then 4 (:123-124) and the takeover fixture really runs everyDeltas=1 (:143,:151); Sequencer's contract sentences are quoted correctly (:105-108, :24-50) and DefaultIngest really completes exceptionally when the returned delta lacks the stream (:359-362). Four majors remain, all in the rows a future session will act on rather than in what was cut: the moved anchor rests on a claim about CheckpointWriterContentTest that I measured false and on a remedy that is unachievable without the row it was moved out of; the decomposition puts the deciding ADR in a different commit from the format change while citing the rule that forbids exactly that; M4.10b's four properties contain no request-rate constraint, and a mechanism that multiplies the commit-path PUT rate by the pod count satisfies all four; and M4.10c states a false fact about how a CommitDelta is versioned today, which is the fact its own cost estimate turns on. Not landable as staged.

findings.title: The moved anchor's premise is false as written, and the remedy it derives is unachievable under the mechanism the same row prescribes -- so the anchor is not the unconditional, format-change-free thing lines 257-264 claim
findings.failure_scenario: Measured, both halves. (a) 'the inverted assertion goes green without the fold' is false. Nothing in any src/main reads Checkpoint.pods() (grep across all modules returns zero hits), CheckpointWriter.pods is a fresh empty HashMap per instance (CheckpointWriter.java:78), and lastWritten() reads the LAST checkpoint body PUT to the store, which after the successor's commit is the successor's own (CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:65-68,151-155). So inverting :156 to containsEntry("poda", 42L) is RED today at everyDeltas=1 and green only once something folds the recovered window in -- the fixture already discriminates exactly the mutation the row says it cannot see. (b) The remedy built on that false premise -- 'that setting must change, and the asserted value must be one only a post-checkpoint commit could supply' -- cannot be satisfied by M4.10d alone. Raise everyDeltas above 1 and the ancestor's commits after its last checkpoint have their flushSeq nowhere durable: CommitDelta carries (sequence, segments) and no pod attribution, and ADR-0033 deliberately keeps the offset-to-segment index out of the checkpoint. Under the mechanism this row itself names (fold into Checkpoint.pods, which 'already exists'), no object holds that value, so no assertion can demand it. The same collision reaches backlog.md:125's 'returning the ORIGINAL offsets': across a takeover the original offsets for a replayed segment live only in a delta nobody can locate without either an index (growth, forbidden by ADR-0033) or a scan (the unbounded replay M4.9 removed). Concretely: a session that lands M4.10b with 'no format change', then picks up M4.10d, raises K, finds no value it can assert, and takes one of the two exits the decomposition exists to prevent -- weaken the anchor assertion (testing.md rule 5, the inversion this row names two lines earlier) or pull the format change into M4.10d, which breaks one-task-one-commit and empties M4.10c. Note also that backlog-notes.md:186-187 already says d 'DEPENDS on M4.10c's outcome', which contradicts :257's 'it needs NO format change'. Remedy: delete :266-269 (the fixture as it stands is already the discriminator, and a deletion cannot add a claim), and state M4.10d's honest reach -- a checkpoint-carried window is stale by up to K deltas or T seconds at the moment of takeover, so a residual duplicate window survives unless M4.10b's answer puts the token somewhere the post-checkpoint deltas carry.

findings.title: The split puts the deciding ADR in M4.10b and the format change in M4.10c, which is what non-negotiable 8 -- cited two lines above to justify the split -- forbids
findings.failure_scenario: :180-182 argues the format change must be its own commit because 'non-negotiable 8 requires it land atomically with its ADR, goldens, readers, writers and fakes'. :184-185 then assigns the ADR to M4.10b and the format change to M4.10c, so the one thing the cited rule binds together is the one thing the split separates. wire-format-change/SKILL.md's checklist item is 'ADR written and travelling in this commit', and adr/SKILL.md says of a wire-format change 'Required, not optional, and it travels in the same commit as the change'. Concretely: a session finishes M4.10b concluding 'the pods key gains a qualifier and CommitDelta gains a field', and commits an accepted ADR describing bytes the tree does not write. Between that commit and M4.10c the tree contradicts an accepted ADR -- the divergence adr/SKILL.md says must then be recorded as a dated Status note -- and M4.10c cannot tick its own checklist item because its ADR landed a commit earlier. The row gives no way out: it does not say M4.10c amends or supersedes, does not say M4.10b's ADR lands as 'proposed', and does not say b and c collapse into one commit when the answer is yes. Remedy is one clause, not a round of prose: say which commit carries the ADR when the answer is 'the format changes' -- the honest answer being that M4.10b's deliverable is then the ADR *plus* the change, i.e. b and c are one commit and c is only ever a separate row in the void case.

findings.title: None of the four properties constrains a request RATE, and the one that looks like it constrains cost constrains object SIZE instead
findings.failure_scenario: The four properties are: answered not merely detected, no object grows with history, survives checkpoint truncation and a leader change, and says which formats change. Growth is not rate, and this is the project's central invariant (non-negotiable 6; cost.md R1, R6: 'commit/metadata write rate is independent of index count', request rates scale with segments, AZs and nodes, never with records or pods). A mechanism that satisfies all four and is a serious cost regression: 'each pod's lastAppliedFlushSeq lives in its own small object at ctl/pods/<podId>, rewritten on every commit'. It is answered (the object can carry the offsets), it never grows with history (fixed size, overwritten), it survives truncation and a leader change (it is outside the chain entirely), and it says plainly which formats change. It also multiplies the commit-path PUT rate by the pod count, which is precisely the per-pod write rate M4.7 exists to remove and the dimension the cost model's $52/partition/month argument turns on. The deleted round-5 sentence carried the only request-rate words in the row ('one GET'), and its replacement carried none; the reason it was deleted -- taking pod attribution into the chain 'reinstates the unbounded replay M4.9 removed' -- now survives only in baselines/review.txt, which is an argued-findings archive that no session picking up M4.10b reads. Remedy: one more property, stated as scope and not as mechanism -- the decision adds no object-store request on the commit path, and answering a replay costs a bounded number of requests that does not scale with pods, records or chain length. That is exactly the M4.9 bound this row could otherwise undo.

findings.title: 'CommitDelta is a ChainEntry under VERSION_KINDED = 1' is false for the delta the shipped path actually writes, and it is the fact M4.10c's budget and M4.10b's cost comparison rest on
findings.failure_scenario: CommitDelta.encode branches on segments.size(): one segment emits ChainEntry.VERSION_DELTA (v0), with no kind byte at all; two or more emit VERSION_KINDED under KIND_DELTA (format/.../CommitDelta.java:144-155). ChainEntry's own javadoc says so explicitly and records that an earlier paragraph got the same thing backwards ('One segment still emits v0, byte-for-byte, so no bucket churns and both golden files stand'). Today every delta the production path writes is v0: DefaultIngest calls sequencer.commit with a single request (DefaultIngest.java:349) and M4.7c records that nothing constructs a BatchingSequencer outside its own test. So a field added to the delta must be added to TWO encodings, or single-segment deltas must move to v1 -- which churns the byte-stability ADR-0032 preserved and the v0 golden M3.0's own precedent (quoted four lines below, at :245-246) says must stay untouched. The delta lives in two versions, not one, which is the same shape as the round-1 finding that the key lives in two formats, not one. Concretely: the M4.10b ADR weighs 'the delta is already kinded and its version path is open, so putting the qualifier there is cheap' against a checkpoint change, chooses the delta, and M4.10c then discovers it owes a v2 encoder, a reader that still accepts v0 and v1, a new golden and the old one intact -- the cost the paragraph at :248-250 exists to make visible for the checkpoint side and hides on this one. Correcting the sentence costs a clause; the ADR it distorts is the expensive artefact.

findings.title: 'Only the timestamp survives a restart' reads against the row's own primary argument seven lines above
findings.failure_scenario: :196-197 says podShortId is stable across a restart, which is the whole hazard; :203 then says only the timestamp survives one. The intended sense is 'only the timestamp still DISCRIMINATES between incarnations', and the parenthetical about SegmentPublisher.sequence being an instance AtomicLong makes it recoverable, but a reader who takes :203 literally concludes podShortId does not survive a restart -- the opposite of the fact the ADR must reason from. Cheap to say directly: podShortId survives and is therefore useless as a discriminator, the sequence resets, so the timestamp is the only part of a SegmentKey that separates two incarnations of one pod -- and only at millisecond granularity, which is also all that SegmentPublisher's uncoordinated `put` (SegmentPublisher.java:136-141) relies on.

findings.title: ambiguousPut/duplicatePut are attributed to CommitProtocolSimulation, where neither identifier appears
findings.failure_scenario: Both are components of FaultInjectingStore.Faults (FaultInjectingStore.java:60) and are drawn there; CommitProtocolSimulation only takes a Faults record as a parameter and hands it to the store (:97,:109-112). A session that greps CommitProtocolSimulation for the named seam finds nothing and has to go looking -- the same 'named object does not contain the named thing' failure the rounds:M0.76 entry in this very file records twice. Naming FaultInjectingStore, and saying that CommitProtocolSimulation is what drives it, costs three words. The substantive claim around it is correct and I verified it: the simulation's driver issues a fresh flushSeq per pod per attempt (CommitProtocolSimulation.java:147,:220-222), so nothing anywhere replays a pair today.
